prompt: In a bridge truss, triangles $ABD$ and $CBD$ share the side $\overline{BD}$. The builder knows $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ and $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$, and nothing about the angles. Which criterion proves $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$? Answer with three letters.
hint: You are given two pairs of congruent sides. Is there a third pair hiding in the picture?

hints.text: You are given two pairs of congruent sides. Is there a third pair hiding in the picture?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Count the pairs on a smaller version: with only $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ plus the shared $\overline{BD}$ you have just two side pairs — not enough. The second given pair makes three sides and zero angles.
The shared side $\overline{BD}$ is congruent to itself by the Reflexive Property — that is your third pair.
Three pairs of sides and no angles: SSS.

explanation: Two pairs of congruent sides are given: $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ and $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$.
The shared side supplies a third pair: $\overline{BD} \cong \overline{BD}$ by the Reflexive Property.
That is three pairs of corresponding sides and no angle information, so the criterion is SSS.

alternativeExplanations.title: Always hunt for the free part
steps: Whenever two triangles share a side or an angle, that shared part is a free congruence, courtesy of the Reflexive Property.
Mark it in the figure before you count. Here it turns "two sides" into the three you need.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is SAS. Students see two sides and assume the angle at $B$ or $D$ is "obviously" congruent — but no angle was given or marked, and looking congruent proves nothing.
Only count parts you were GIVEN or can justify with a property. Given sides, given sides, reflexive side: that is SSS.
